title: The Discount Airtime Rule — and Who Counts as a Candidate
hook: U.S. law forces broadcasters to sell candidates ad time at their lowest rate near an election. The 2026 fight is not over the discount, but over who gets to claim it.
key_points: Under 47 U.S.C. 315, broadcasters must offer candidates their lowest unit charge — the cheapest rate any advertiser pays for the same slot.
The window is limited: 45 days before a primary and 60 days before a general election.
The rule aims to keep the cost of reaching voters from depending on a campaign's bargaining power with stations.
An FCC public notice in March 2026 extended the preferential rate to political parties and joint fundraising committees, per SCOTUSblog.
A divided 4th Circuit panel held the statute unambiguous — the discount belongs to a candidate, not to party committees.

The NRCC and NRSC asked the Supreme Court on August 31, 2026 to pause that ruling with the midterms about two months away; Judge Wilkinson had dissented below, warning it restricts speech near an election.
content_html: Buying airtime is one of the largest costs in a modern campaign, and U.S. law has long tried to keep that cost from turning on how much leverage a campaign has with a television station. The tool is the lowest unit charge: near an election, broadcasters must sell candidates time at the cheapest rate they give anyone.
extra_html: SCOTUSblog's Amy Howe reports that the fight in 2026 is not about the discount itself but about who may claim it. Under 47 U.S.C. 315 the preferential rate runs in the 45 days before a primary and the 60 days before a general election; an FCC public notice in March 2026 extended it beyond candidates to political parties and joint fundraising committees. A divided panel of the 4th Circuit held that the statute is unambiguous and that the benefit belongs to "a candidate" for their own use, not to party committees. On August 31, 2026, the National Republican Congressional Committee and National Republican Senatorial Committee asked the Supreme Court to temporarily pause that decision, noting the midterms were just over two months off; Judge Wilkinson, dissenting below, argued the ruling restricts political speech in a sensitive pre-election period. Two general points sit underneath the specifics. First, a subsidy defined for one class of speaker immediately raises the question of who else resembles that class closely enough to qualify — parties spend on behalf of candidates, but they are not candidates. Second, when a benefit only exists inside a short window, the speed of judicial relief is the relief, which is why disputes like this land on the emergency docket. (This card describes U.S. broadcast and campaign law specifically.)

related.title: The Distinction That Could Reshape Super PACs
related.hook: Citizens United protects unlimited independent spending. Maine's law doesn't touch spending — it caps what one donor may give the committee doing the spending. That gap is now in court.

related.title: Why Outside Money Loves a Primary
related.hook: A dollar spent in a low-turnout primary buys far more influence than the same dollar in a general election — which is where super PACs increasingly aim it.

related.title: The Free Press & Democracy
related.hook: A free press is sometimes called the "fourth estate" — an unofficial branch of power whose job is to watch the other three on the public's behalf.

related.title: The Supreme Court's Other Docket
related.hook: The Court hears about sixty argued cases a year and disposes of thousands more by short written order. Most of what it does never gets an opinion at all.

flashcards.prompt: What is the lowest unit charge rule?
flashcards.back_html: A federal requirement that broadcasters sell candidates airtime at the cheapest rate any advertiser pays for a comparable slot, during a window before primary and general elections.

flashcards.prompt: What is the 2026 dispute about the discount rate actually over?

choices.text: Whether party committees, not just candidates, can claim the preferential rate
Whether broadcasters must run political ads at all
Whether the discount applies to newspaper advertising

flashcards.explanation_html: The FCC extended it to parties and joint fundraising committees; the 4th Circuit read the statute as covering only a candidate.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the timing of the emergency application matter?

choices.text: The discount window is short and the midterms were about two months away, so a delayed ruling decides the practical outcome
The Supreme Court cannot hear election cases in even-numbered years
Broadcasters set all rates on January 1 and cannot change them

flashcards.explanation_html: When relief only matters inside a 45- or 60-day window, how fast a court acts is itself the remedy — which is why the committees went to the emergency docket.
